comparator.name: Landscape Architecture and Planning
comparator.sourceNotes: The current official handbook defines 180 EC: a 96-EC common part, a 54-EC specialisation and 30 EC of open electives. Landscape Architecture is selected by neutral official-order tie-break; the three common-part restricted choices use their first-listed options. The optional 24-EC internship is not part of the fixed 180-EC pathway.

routeSelection.basis: The generic target has two equally formal 54-EC specialisations, Landscape Architecture and Spatial Planning. Neither is identified as the general route, so the first current handbook specialisation is selected neutrally and independently of UCR fit.

alternatives.label: Landscapes, people & spatial sustainability
alternatives.concept: A closest feasible landscape-planning response combining human geography, environmental systems, water, spatial evidence, economics, governance and applied sustainability research.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum combines social and environmental systems, spatial data, water, economics, governance and applied sustainability research around places and landscapes.
progression: Social-science, sustainability, data and research foundations precede water, earth observation, environmental systems, economics, governance and applied landscape research. Formal prerequisites and planned offerings pass; eight 300-level courses are included.

alternatives.label: Landscape ecology, climate & spatial evidence
alternatives.concept: Develops the evidenced landscape-architecture and climate-adaptation direction through ecology, water, soils, climate, earth observation and spatial environmental research, while acknowledging the absence of professional design studios.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum centres ecology, climate, water, soils, hazards, earth observation, geospatial analysis and environmental research.
progression: Ecology, earth-system, water, climate and data foundations precede soils, hazards, earth observation, environmental systems and advanced applied research. Formal prerequisites and planned offerings pass; eight 300-level courses are included.
alternatives.distinctness: This route makes landscape ecology, climate adaptation and geospatial environmental evidence the organising priority. It differs from the closest programme by ten courses and 75 EC.

alternatives.label: Spatial planning, governance & participation
alternatives.concept: Develops the official Spatial Planning direction through institutions, land-use conflict, law, public policy, economics, participation and communication.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum centres sociology, politics, law, economics, stakeholder communication and public decision-making around inclusive and sustainable places.
alternatives.distinctness: This route makes institutions, participation, law and planning governance the organising priority. It differs from the closest programme by ten courses and from the landscape-ecology direction by twenty courses.
progression: Sociology, politics, law, economics and research foundations precede planning governance, public decision-making, rights, stakeholder communication and advanced policy study. Formal prerequisites and planned offerings pass; eight 300-level courses are included.

How can ecological, water, soil and climate evidence inform landscape interventions?

selection.assessment: The closest programme integrates landscapes, society, environmental systems and spatial evidence. Landscape ecology/climate and spatial planning/governance support two further coherent, feasible and pairwise-distinct directions. Production stops at the three-alternative maximum.

blocks: Both introduce sustainability and human-environment perspectives on landscapes and spatial change.
Both develop geospatial and Earth-observation analysis.
Both examine water systems and the consequences of spatial and environmental management choices.
Both integrate Earth-system evidence across spatial scales, while WUR provides dedicated landscape geography.
Both use interdisciplinary applied research to address a real spatial sustainability problem, without claiming design-studio equivalence.
Both analyse governance and decision processes for sustainability, though WUR integrates formal planning-and-design theory.
Both examine working with natural processes in environmental interventions.
Both establish introductory ecology and biodiversity knowledge.
Both study soils and subsurface conditions that shape landscapes.
Both examine people, institutions and social patterns in relation to places.
Both examine institutions and structured public decision-making, while WUR adds studio planning practice.
Both introduce economic reasoning about allocation, incentives and competing land-use interests.

notes.text: WUR offers a professional landscape-architecture and planning curriculum with repeated design studios, representation, planting and construction, landscape engineering, aesthetics, regional design and a dedicated thesis. UCR can combine substantial environmental science, spatial evidence, economics, sociology and governance, but does not reproduce professional landscape-architecture studio training.
